candidates.raw_excerpt: Venus is at its most dazzling in the predawn sky this week as it shines close to the bright star Spica in the southeast. Here's what you need to know. As an inner planet, Venus never strays far from the horizon, at least compared to outer planets like Jupiter and Mars which can be visible all night long during opposition, when they shine opposite the sun in Earth's sky. Instead, Venus alternates between morning and evening appearances. All the while, its shifting moon-like phases and ever-changing proximity to Earth causes its brightness to wax and wane. When is Venus at its most dazzling? Venus will reach peak brightness during its current morning apparition at 1:37 p.m. EST (1837 GMT) on Nov. 27 according to the astronomy website In-The-Sky . Stargazers in the U.S. could get an incredible view of Venus in the predawn hours of the coming week, as the planet climbs into the southeastern sky ahead of the rising sun, with Mercury clinging close to the horizon below. Spica is a double system of two stars that orbit one another once every four days. Its stars are separated by just approximately 11 million miles (less than 18 million kilometers), making them far too close to split visually with even the most powerful amateur equipment. candidates.title: Rocket Lab sending Japanese satellite to orbit on Thanksgiving Day launch: Watch it live
candidates.raw_excerpt: Rocket Lab will add another satellite to a growing Japanese Earth-observation constellation today (Nov. 26), and you can watch the action live. An Electron rocket carrying a radar imaging satellite for Tokyo-based Earth-observation company Synspective is scheduled to lift off from Rocket Lab 's New Zealand launch site today, during a window that opens at 7:00 p.m. ET (0000 GMT and 1:00 p.m. on Nov. 27 in New Zealand). You can watch the mission, called "Night Owls Never Sleep," via Rocket Lab starting about 30 minutes before liftoff. Space.com will carry the company's stream if, as expected, it's made available. Synspective is building a network of "Strix" spacecraft equipped with synthetic aperture radar (SAR), which uses radio waves to generate detailed images of Earth's surface in both day and night lighting, as well as through cloud cover. Today's launch will be Rocket Lab's 14th for Synspective to date, and there are a lot more coming. At the end of September, Rocket Lab announced a deal with the company for an additional 20 Electron missions between 2028 and 2031 — the largest commercial launch contract in the rocket's history. That agreement brought Synspective's total number of contracted Electron flights to 47. Synspective aims to eventually establish a constellation capable of imaging locations anywhere on Earth at intervals of just a few hours. The patch for Rocket Lab's "Night Owls Never Sleep" mission. (Image credit: Rocket Lab) If all goes to plan today, the Electron's kick stage will deploy the Strix satellite into low Earth orbit , 569 kilometers (353.6 miles) above our planet. "Night Owl Never Sleeps" will be the 101st mission to date for Rocket Lab. candidates.raw_excerpt: An image captured by the Dark Energy Camera showcasing the Betta Fish Nebula. (Image credit: CTIO/NOIRLab/DOE/NSF/AURA) The striking blue of the Betta Fish Nebula swims across the cosmic landscape, a stunning wisp of material leftover from a stellar explosion. What is it? Roughly 6,800 light-years from Earth and nestled in the Centaurus constellation, this piece of the supernova remnant SNR G295.5+09.7 has earned the nickname the Betta Fish Nebula for its floaty, fishy shape. This almost ghostly whirl of gas and dust was created when a star much more massive than our sun exploded, blasting its outer layers of material outward in the process. Over time, the remnants of this supernova eruption stretched outward into space, dispersing and colliding with surrounding gas. Transport shapes how people live, work and trade. As cities grow and international commerce expands, making travel cleaner, more efficient and accessible to everyone has become an urgent global priority.

In cities, replacing gas-guzzling cars with electric ones is just one step towards greener daily journeys. To truly reduce car dependence, commuters need reliable public transit, safe cycling routes and seamless links between different modes of transport.

Chinese astronauts Tang Hongbo, Wu Yi, and Pakistani astronaut Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, of the Shenzhou 24 crew entered the China Space Station on Wednesday. Ali became the first foreign astronaut to board the space station.

Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said Wednesday that China is ready to work with Pakistan and other countries to deepen international cooperation in space, improve global governance of outer space, and ensure that the benefits of space exploration are shared more broadly by all humanity.

"We are ready to deepen exchanges and cooperation with more countries and regions in areas such as joint astronaut selection and training, scientific experiments and more," Zhou Yaqiang, chief systems designer of the General Technology Department of the China Manned Space Agency, told CGTN.

The China Space Station has abundant resources for scientific experiments, stable in-orbit operational capabilities, a mature space transportation system for travel to and from the station, and a well-established astronaut selection and training system. The country is also advancing its lunar exploration program according to plan. 

"Together, we can promote the rapid development of space technology, explore the vast universe, and benefit all humanity," Zhou said.

candidates.title: European spacecraft finds chaotic scene after asteroid deflection experiment
candidates.raw_excerpt: Four years ago, NASA dispatched a small spacecraft on a suicide mission to show how humanity might deflect an asteroid on a collision course with Earth. The first-of-its-kind experiment worked beautifully as the solar-powered space probe slammed into asteroid Dimorphos, permanently altering its trajectory. Using telescopes, astronomers measured changes in the orbit of Dimorphos around a larger asteroid companion named Didymos in the aftermath of NASA's Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) mission. The spacecraft released some 10 billion joules of energy as it impacted Dimorphos in September 2022 at more than 13,700 mph (6.14 kilometers per second), shortening the asteroid's 12-hour orbit around Didymos by about 33 minutes, 25 times the most conservative expectation. But scientists could only learn so much from DART. The collision destroyed the spacecraft, as expected. candidates.title: December full moon 2026: When, where and how to see the Cold Moon
candidates.raw_excerpt: The December full moon reaches peak illumination at 8:28 p.m. EST on Dec. 23 (0128 GMT on Dec. 24) as the lunar disk shines opposite the sun in Earth's sky. It is often called the "Cold Moon" in reference to the frigid temperatures that prevail in the Northern Hemisphere around the time of its rising, according to the Old Farmer's Almanac . December's full moon will also occur close to perigee — the moon's closest point to Earth in its elliptical orbit — giving rise to a spectacular supermoon. A supermoon can appear 30% brighter and 14% larger than a full moon at its farthest point from Earth (also known as a micromoon).. According to the late, great astronomer Fred Espenak , the Cold Moon will be just 221,667 miles (356,740 kilometers) from Earth when it turns full, making it the closest supermoon of 2026! When to see the December full moon The full Cold Supermoon will make for a spectacular sight when it rises over the eastern horizon at sunset on Dec. 23, mere hours before reaching maximum illumination. Remember to use Time and Date's moonrise and moonset tracker for timings specific to your location. Earth's satellite may appear larger than normal while close to the horizon. This is partly because it is near perigee, when it appears subtly larger in the night sky, but also because of a phenomenon called the moon illusion, which tricks us into perceiving the moon to be bigger than it actually is while in the presence of foreground objects. A yellow full moon rises over Italy. (Image credit: Photo by Lorenzo Di Cola/NurPhoto via Getty Images) The moon may also adopt a striking golden or orange hue around moonrise and moonset. When the moon is low on the horizon, its light travels through more of Earth's atmopshere, scattering shorter, bluer wavelengths of light and allowing longer, redder wavelengths to reach our eyes. candidates.raw_excerpt: On Nov. 25, 1970, an experimental aircraft called the Northrop M2-F3 made its first powered flight. The M2-F3 aircraft was a heavyweight "lifting body" designed to test its ability to produce most of its lift through its fuselage instead of wings. It's commonly referred to as a "wingless" aircraft. After Air Force test pilot Bill Dana took the M2-F3 on three unpowered glide test flights, he did the first powered flight, too. Dana soared to an altitude of 45,000 feet during this flight, which lasted just over 6 minutes. He didn't break the sound barrier this time, but he did on later flights. The M2-F3 flew a total of 27 missions in its three-year flight history. Its top speed was 1.6 times the speed of sound, and its top altitude was 71,500 feet. NASA's M2-F3 lifting body drops from its carrier plane during a test flight in 1970. (Image credit: NASA) Why it mattered In the late 1960s and early 1970s, NASA was investigating lifting bodies as an approach to both new aircraft and what future spacecraft, and as its number suggests, the M2-F3 was not the first of its kind. In fact, the M2-F3 was a rebuilt version of its predecessor, the M2-F2 lifting body , after that vehicle crashed in a dry lake bed in California's Mojave Desert during an unpowered test flight. That crash (which appears in the opening of the TV show "The Six-Million-Dollar Man") led to upgrades for a better handling lifting body, NASA said. "When the M2-F2 was rebuilt and redesignated the M2-F3, it was modified with an additional third vertical fin – centered between the tip fins – to improve control characteristics," NASA wrote in an overview . candidates.raw_excerpt: Bulgarian satellite manufacturer EnduroSat signed a launch deal with Blue Origin for two dedicated launches on New Glenn, with the first mission targeted for 2029. EnduroSat said the missions will deploy satellites built by the company “for new and existing customers,” with EnduroSat noting recent orders from TrustPoint and Vantor . It marks an interesting shift for the satellite manufacturer to procure launch services for its customers. “Making space universally accessible means removing the biggest bottlenecks our customers face. With two New Glenn missions dedicated entirely to our customers, they can fly larger spacecraft and full constellations, while also scaling faster and working with one partner from concept to orbit,” said Raycho Raychev, founder and CEO of EnduroSat commented. The missions will launch on the standard New Glenn variant, the 7×2 vehicle, which is designed to launch 45 metric tons to Low Earth Orbit (LEO) and 13 metric tons to Geostationary Transfer Orbit (GTO). This is the second launch deal for New Glenn within a week after Google purchased a mission for its Project Suncatcher, also targeted for 2029 . New Glenn is currently grounded as it rebuilds the launch pad and implements fixes after an explosion during a hotfire test over the summer . Now, the spacecraft has revealed that DART flattened one face of Dimorphos with a stadium-sized crater and set it tumbling chaotically. The impact also appears to have blasted out hundreds of previously unknown boulders that are now circling the binary asteroids. "Scientists debated whether Dimorphos had sustained an impact crater, changed its shape, or stayed the same," Hera principal investigator Patrick Michel, Director of Research at the Observatoire de la Côte d'Azur, said in a statement. China has completed a key component for what it calls the world's first 600-megawatt-class compressed-air energy storage system, a technology that stores electricity by compressing air and releases it later to generate power – like a large-scale "air battery."

The component, called an expander, is the core of the system. It turns the energy in stored compressed air into usable power. The developer, the Institute of Engineering Thermophysics under the Chinese Academy of Sciences, worked with Zhongchu Guoneng (Beijing) Technology Co. on the project. The team said the expander has completed integration and mechanical tests and rolled off the production line.

The institute said the machine is fully independently developed, with 100% of its equipment made in China. It is designed to handle changing speeds and wide ranges of demand – features needed for real-world grid use – and offers advantages including high efficiency, fast start-up and shutdown, long service life and easy maintenance. Test results met or exceeded design targets, according to the developer.

Compared with a 300MW-class system, the 600MW-class system is twice as large, cuts unit power cost by 20% to 30% and improves system efficiency by 3% to 5%, said a report from China Media Group.

Compressed-air energy storage is seen as a promising way to help power grids absorb more renewable energy from wind and solar. China's new expander, if deployed at scale, could help make large-scale storage cheaper and more efficient, the developer said, adding that the breakthrough could push global compressed-air storage technology to a new level.

candidates.title: On this day in space! Nov. 24, 1947: The US Navy launches the 1st Aerobee sounding rocket, but it didn't reach space
candidates.raw_excerpt: On Nov. 24, 1947, the U.S. Navy launched the first Aerobee rocket into the sky, but it never reached space. Aerobee was a suborbital sounding rocket designed to study Earth's atmosphere . After World War 2, the United States started reusing erman V-2 rockets for this kind of research. When they started running out of V-2 rockets , the United States constructed its own rockets that were similar but cheaper to build and to launch. In the weeks leading up to the first Aerobee mission, three test flights were launched. Those tests used a dummy version of Aerobee with a live booster to see if the two stages would separate properly. On Aerobee's first real flight, the rocket flew about 35 miles high. That's below the 62-mile (100 kilometers) upper limit for the boundary of space . (NASA and the U.S. military typically consider 50 miles the edge of space.) Mission control cut the flight short after about 30 seconds, because Aerobee started to yaw, and they wanted to keep it from going completely out of control. The first Aerobee sounding rocket launched on Nov. 24, 1947 under a project led by the U.S. Navy. (Image credit: U.S. Navy) Why it mattered Billed as the " most successful sounding rocket of the space age ," the initial Aerobee rocket was suborbital rocket designed to launch experment payload of up to 100 pounds (45 kilograms) to an altitude of 75 miles (121 kilometers) or so. "The Aerobee was designed to carry instruments aloft to collect data on the upper atmosphere and to place small animals in a weightless condition for physiological studies," the U.S. National Museum of the United States Air Force wrote in a mission overview . "It was launched by a solid-propellant booster engine of 18,000 pounds thrust that burned for only two and a half seconds." candidates.raw_excerpt: Amazon Leo now has more than 400 satellites in orbit after a Tuesday morning launch by Arianespace . The French launcher deployed 36 satellites in the mission, just over a week after Amazon lost 40 satellites in a United Launch Alliance (ULA) launch failure . The mission lasted 2 hours and 4 minutes and Arianespace confirmed the satellites were successfully deployed. Arianespace has emerged as a critical partner for Amazon Leo as its other launchers ULA and Blue Origin have struggled. Arianespace launched 136 satellites for the constellation this year across four missions. “Every Ariane 6 mission we fly with Arianespace builds on the one before it,” commented Steve Metayer, Amazon Leo vice president of production. “Our Leo team works side by side with Arianespace on everything from satellite integration to launch day operations, and that shared expertise and trust is the driving force behind our cadence together this year.” Earlier this year, Metayer told journalists that Arianespace “really stepped up” for Amazon, noting the reliability on manifest dates and launch performance. According to an update to ESA’s dedicated Ariane 6 page , the flight is currently expected to take place on 17 December. Should the launch go ahead as planned, Arianespace will have completed six Ariane 6 flights in 2026. candidates.raw_excerpt: As ubiquitous as the sun is to us today, our star is not eternal; one day, albeit in billions of years, it will die. While massive stars die in supernova explosions, the sun and stars of similar mass die quieter deaths. But that doesn't mean these stars completely go out with a whimper. New observations collected using the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA), the world's largest radio telescope comprised of 66 antennas in northern Chile, reveal that the sun's death throes may be different from what scientists had initially believed. NASA Jet Propulsion Lab (JPL) researcher Raghvendra Sahai, who led the investigation, explained the shape the ALMA observations took: "It's essentially a physical snapshot of an event that, until now, we've mostly inferred from theoretical models. We've caught, for the first time, a star's final nuclear heartbeat, frozen in gas." Sun-like stars "die" when they run out of hydrogen in their cores. This means that the fusion of hydrogen to helium ceases in the stellar core, and because this nuclear process is a star's main energy source, the star no longer has the outward push to support itself against the inward push of its own gravity. As the star's core collapses to create a stellar remnant called a white dwarf , the outer layers where hydrogen is still fusing to form helium swell out. This expansion leads to a relatively short-lived " red giant " phase. Eventually, these outer layers will cool and disperse, leaving the central white dwarf surrounded by a so-called "planetary nebula" shell of debris. During the red giant phase, as the stellar core is surrounded by shells of hydrogen and helium, these layers are occasionally rocked by flares in nuclear activity called thermal pulses. During these episodes, stellar material is flung into space. Scientists call Didymos a "rubble pile" asteroid , meaning it's a loose body made up of boulders, dust, gravel and other bits of the solar system held together by the asteroid's own gravity. VI on Monday. The combined company is expected to start trading on the NYSE today under the ticker $QSPC. The deal brought in ~$300M of new capital at an implied pro forma equity value of ~$958M, down from the ~$1.2B Quantum predicted when it announced the merger in June. Quantum plans to pour the cash into production of its Ranger and Scout spacecraft, though Ranger has yet to fly.  In June, CEO Jim Bridenstine said in a press conference that speed drove the choice of a SPAC over a traditional IPO. “We need to go as fast as possible to get these capabilities on-orbit as soon as possible,” he said.  SPAC is back: For years, the word SPAC alone could send industry veterans back to the frothy days of 2021, when several companies went public via SPAC only to fail, giving the vehicle a bad rap. But just like Y2K (both fashion and computer conspiracies), SPACs have also made a comeback, with Quantum being the third space company to close one since October. NorthStar Earth & Space ($NSTR) closed its $300M merger with Viking Acquisition Corp. I on Oct. 1, alongside a $30M PIPE. The stock peaked at $5.95 on its first day of trading and now trades at ~$1.62. WISeSat.Space ($SAIQ) closed the same day at a $250M base equity valuation plus a $10M PIPE. Shares spiked to $9.94 four days later and have since sunk to ~$2.70. The trend seems unlikely to slow down, as several other space companies also recently announced SPAC deals which have not yet been finalized, including Ursa Major ($2.3B), Astrum Space (~$1B), Astro Digital (~$587M enterprise value), and Space-Eyes ($638M). The robotic Progress 97 cargo craft launched atop a Soyuz rocket from the Russia-run Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan today (Nov. 24) at 5:17 a.m. EST (1013 GMT; 3:17 p.m. Baikonur time), carrying several tons of supplies for the astronauts aboard the orbiting lab. If all goes to plan, Progress 97 will arrive at the International Space Station (ISS) on Thursday (Nov. 26), docking with its Poisk module. But the freighter will then hop over to a different port, according to journalist and space historian Anatoly Zak: the aft one of the PrK transfer tunnel, which leads to Russia's Zvezda service module. The PrK port is the best site for engine burns that boost the orbit of the ISS, a service that Progress freighters regularly provide. candidates.raw_excerpt: A think tank is urging Congress to act to protect critical infrastructure for space operations in a new report released today. The Foundation for Defense of Democracies argued that space is critical to the American way of life, from PNT to weather forecasting to communications—and that interruption of these services would be detrimental to national security. However, policy to designate space as critical infrastructure in the same way as the electric grid or financial systems has lagged behind this technical reality.  The threats: Adversaries, including China and Russia, are already hard at work developing and testing tech to deny US entities access to space, through nonkinetic tactics such as jamming and spoofing as well as physical assaults such as anti-satellite missiles or maneuvering of spacecraft. “Looking ahead, the most damaging scenario may not be kinetic attacks on satellites, but a prolonged campaign of difficult-to-attribute interference that gradually reduces confidence in American navigation, communications, imagery, and warning data,” the report predicted. Ask of Congress: The report’s top recommendation to Congress is to designate space-based systems as the 17th critical infrastructure sector. candidates.title: China to extend its longest spaceflight record with a year-long stay
candidates.raw_excerpt:
China is set to break its longest spaceflight record, allowing astronaut Zhu Yangzhu, a member of the Shenzhou-23 mission crew, to spend a full year in orbit, the China Manned Space Agency (CMSA) announced on Tuesday.

Zhu will remain aboard the China Space Station through the Shenzhou-24 crew rotation. Both missions are scheduled to last six months.

"This is by no means a simple accumulation of two six-month missions," CMSA spokesperson Zhang Jingbo said at a press conference at the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwest China.

Zhang said the year-long stay is designed to pursue two objectives: establishing a new human space research system to study how the body adapts to and changes under spaceflight conditions, and systematically validating the station's capacity to support an astronaut's health, work and daily life over an extended period.

A stress test

Bone loss alone proceeds at 1% to 2% per month in microgravity. Even with roughly two hours of daily exercise aboard the International Space Station (ISS), astronauts can still lose significant muscle mass during shorter missions. A continuous year in orbit eliminates the physiological "reset" that occurs when astronauts return to Earth between separate flights, allowing researchers to observe whether these changes plateau, worsen or trigger new adaptation mechanisms.

The technical foundation for extended stays is China's regenerative environmental control and life support system. candidates.title: BepiColombo Enters Orbit Around Mercury Despite “Software Glitch”
candidates.raw_excerpt: Credit: ESA The European Space Agency’s BepiColombo mission has successfully entered orbit around Mercury despite a software glitch that resulted in a shorter-than-planned thruster burn. According to the agency’s 23 November update, the BepiColombo spacecraft reoriented itself at 17:51 CET on 21 November, resulting in a planned loss of communications with Earth. At 19:24 CET, the spacecraft fired its four chemical thrusters as it passed approximately 635 kilometres above Mercury’s surface. The burn was scheduled to last 37 minutes, with communications expected to resume at 22:37 CET. However, the agency did not publicly confirm that contact had been re-established until 03:02 CET on 22 November. In its initial update, the agency confirmed that the spacecraft had achieved orbital capture around Mercury and that ground teams were assessing telemetry. According to ESA’s subsequent account of the manoeuvre, orbital capture had been confirmed internally at approximately 01:00 CET. It was not until 20:15 CET on 22 November that the agency revealed that the thruster burn had been shorter than planned due to a software issue. In a more detailed breakdown published on 23 November, ESA explained that when it re-established contact with the spacecraft, teams discovered that it had entered safe mode. “Upon finding Bepi in safe mode, it was like flipping a switch. Everybody was focused in understanding what had happened,” said ESA’s BepiColombo flight operations director Ignacio Tanco. Teams at ESA and spacecraft manufacturer Airbus have traced the anomaly to a software issue affecting the spacecraft’s orientation and thruster control, although investigations are ongoing. According to ESA, the burn achieved just 77% of its intended change in velocity. While this did not prevent the spacecraft from achieving orbital capture, it entered a 75-hour orbit around Mercury instead of the planned 58-hour orbit. candidates.title: China, Pakistan to conduct cooperative space station experiments
candidates.raw_excerpt:
China and Pakistan will conduct four cooperative scientific experiments aboard China Space Station, involving cyanobacteria, quinoa seeds and two types of composite materials, according to  the Technology and Engineering Center for Space Utilization of Chinese Academy of Sciences.

The Pakistani astronaut on a short-term flight on China Space Station will carry out related experimental operations in orbit.

One of the experiments, proposed by Pakistan’s Space and Upper Atmosphere Research Commission, will examine how cyanobacteria grow and absorb carbon dioxide in space, providing data for future oxygen regeneration and biological production. Cyanobacteria are tiny organisms that use sunlight to grow and release oxygen. The organisms used in the experiment come from Pakistan.

Another experiment, led by the University of Agriculture Faisalabad, will expose 32 quinoa seed samples to the space environment to study their resilience and longevity.

Two materials experiments will test the protective performance of graphene-based composites and the repair efficiency of self-healing carbon fiber composites.

The Pakistani astronaut Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, who will take a short-term flight on China Space Station, will carry out related experimental operations in orbit, according to Chen Mengyun, International Cooperation Project Manager at the Technology and Engineering Center for Space Utilization of Chinese Academy of Sciences.

Chinese and Pakistani scientific teams will also jointly publish papers and share the results of the experiments, said Chen.

The space station will continue to solicit, select and implement new space science projects, Chen said.

She added that China Space Station, also the national space laboratory, is open to scientists worldwide. It solicits proposals for space science and application projects from global scientists on an ongoing basis each year.
